label: SIMULATED pilot. Coded by the specialist (an AI) with the frozen rubric (protocol/partC-rubric.md). One coder. Does not evaluate any Part C threshold.

S2_impersonation_read_correctly.note: All six said scammers were imitating the name. But next steps for Ana ('Avoid, check official site first') and Graduate ('be wary') lean toward avoidance of the brand.

S4_nothing_found_resolved_treated_as_cle.note: Lee: 'company is legit. Proceed to apply.' Ana: 'legit company'. Graduate said 'safe so far' and planned more research (coded not clean-treating, borderline).

S3_complaint_alert_read_as_regulator_fin.note: All six said it was not a regulator action; next steps ranged from 'check reviews' to 'still avoid' (Lee) to 'ignore' (Analyst).

S1_read_as_confirmed_regulator_action.note: Several over-read a suspension: 'likely illegal to hire' (Lee), 'not allowed to operate' (Min, Analyst), 'can't hire here' (Raj).

wording_observations: The stimuli carry an explicit label sentence ('This warning is about people imitating the brand', 'not a finding by a regulator'). Simulated readers echo the label, so the pilot cannot show whether real readers would read it without such a sentence. It does show the draft wording is at least parseable.

'No red flags found' (S4) invited 'legit' and 'proceed to apply' from 2 of 6. The word 'Nothing found in the sources checked' was paraphrased as 'no red flags' by most; consider wording that names what was NOT checked.
A suspended licence (S1) was over-read as 'illegal / not allowed to operate'; wording should say exactly what the status means.
